english.title: My Grandmother's Recipe Book
paras: My grandmother never measured anything. When I asked her how much flour went into her bread, she would hold out a cupped hand and {1|say, "About this much".} For years I assumed her recipes existed only in her memory.

Then, while helping her move into a smaller apartment, I found a notebook wedged behind the spice rack. Its pages {2|was} stiff with flour and stained with tea. {3|Inside, it was} dozens of recipes written in three languages: Urdu, English, and a shorthand that only she could read.

{4|Although} I had expected exact quantities, the notebook was full of notes like "until it smells right" and "add more if the weather is dry." At first I was disappointed. {5|} Gradually, however, I realized that the notebook recorded something more valuable than measurements: it recorded {6|her judgment, her patience, and how she paid attention.}

That winter, I tried to make her bread on my own. My first loaf was dense and pale; {7|my second loaf, which was the next one I made after the first,} was only slightly better. By the fifth attempt, I had begun to notice the things she had written about: the way the dough {8|changes} when it has been kneaded enough, the smell of yeast that is ready.
Now when friends ask me for the recipe, I hand them a copy of the notebook {9|but explaining} that the most important ingredient is not written anywhere. {10|}

english.title: Mary Anning, Fossil Hunter
paras: In the early 1800s, the cliffs near Lyme Regis, on England's southern coast, were constantly crumbling into the sea. For most residents, the landslides were a nuisance. For Mary Anning, {11|they were an opportunity}.

Anning's family was poor, and she began searching the beach for fossils as a child, selling them to tourists to help pay the family's bills. Around 1811, she and her brother Joseph uncovered the skeleton of an {12|ichthyosaur; a} marine reptile that had lived more than 200 million years earlier. {13|Scientists, which were eager to study such creatures,} soon began visiting her shop.

Over the following decades, Anning made discoveries that changed how scientists understood the history of life. She found the first complete plesiosaur skeleton and some of the earliest pterosaur fossils found in Britain. {14|Their} careful observations also helped show that certain stones, called coprolites, were fossilized dung.

Despite these achievements, Anning received little formal recognition during her lifetime. Women could not join the Geological Society of London, {15|and} the scientists who bought her fossils often published descriptions of them without mentioning her name. {16|Therefore,} many of those same scientists relied on her expertise and visited her to discuss their work.

Today, Anning is widely celebrated. {17|Statues, books and, films} tell her story, and her fossils can be seen in major museums. {18|Her life is a reminder that discoveries depend not only on luck but also on skill, persistence, and knowing where to look.}

[1] Visitors to Lyme Regis can still walk the beaches where she worked. [2] Every winter storm exposes new fossils. [3] Fossil hunters, many of them inspired by Anning, {19|searching the shoreline} in all kinds of weather. {20|}

english.title: The Night Market
paras: In many cities, when the offices close and the evening air cools, {21|empty parking lots transform into} night markets. Within an hour, rows of stalls appear, {22|each one lit by strings of bulbs, the smell of grilled corn drifting} between them.

Night markets {23|have exist} for centuries, and they serve purposes that go beyond shopping. For small vendors, they offer a low-cost way to reach customers without renting a permanent shop. For residents, they {24|provides} a place to meet neighbors, try unfamiliar food, and enjoy the city after dark.

Researchers who study urban life point out that night markets can also make streets {25|safer because} more people are present in public spaces in the evening. {26|Busy sidewalks give residents more "eyes on the street,"} an idea popularized by the urban writer Jane Jacobs, who argued that lively streets discourage crime.

Running a successful market, however, {27|requires} careful planning. Organizers must arrange permits, provide lighting and waste collection, and balance the needs of vendors with those of nearby residents, {28|which may object to noise and traffic.}

When these details are handled well, a night market becomes more than a place to buy things. {29|It turns an ordinary space into a shared one. Where people who might never otherwise meet stand} in the same line for the same bowl of noodles. {30|}

english.title: Learning to Fail Forward
paras: Our school's robotics club had one goal for the regional competition: to build a robot that could pick up a ball and drop it into a basket. {31|} We had six weeks, a box of parts, and almost no experience.

Our first design used a claw made of two metal arms. {32|It looked impressive, it dropped the ball} every time the robot moved. Our second design, a scoop, {33|worked better} but was too slow. With two weeks left, we were running out of ideas.

That was when our coach asked us to stop building and start {34|writing}. She had each of us list every problem we had seen and every guess about its cause. Reading the lists aloud, we discovered that three of us had noticed the same thing: the ball was slightly heavier than the specifications said. {35|Our claw had been designed for a ball that did not exist.}
{36|Armed with this information, a new gripper was designed by the team} using rubber pads that could hold the extra weight. {37|It had worked} on the very first test.

We finished fourth at the competition, which was not the result we had hoped for. {38|Yet} I learned more from that season than from any trophy. I learned that a failure is often just information that has not yet been {39|read and, that} the most useful question after a mistake is not "Who is to blame?" but "What is this telling us?" {40|}

english.title: The Science of Sourdough
paras: Long before packaged yeast was sold in stores, bakers made bread rise using a sourdough starter: a simple mixture of flour and water {41|which, has been left} to ferment. Today, many home bakers are rediscovering this ancient method.

A starter is alive. It contains wild yeasts and lactic acid bacteria that feed on the sugars in flour. {42|As the yeasts feed, they release carbon dioxide gas, which becomes trapped in the dough and makes it rise.} The bacteria, meanwhile, produce acids that give sourdough its tangy flavor {43|and help keeping} the bread fresh for longer.

Keeping a starter healthy {44|have required} regular feeding. A baker removes part of the starter and adds fresh flour and water, usually once a day. {45|When the starter neglects,} the microbes run out of food, and the starter may develop an unpleasant smell or a layer of liquid on top.

Because every kitchen contains a slightly different mix of microbes, no two starters are exactly alike. A starter made in a humid coastal city may taste different from one made in a dry mountain town. {46|However,} some bakers describe their starters almost as if they were pets, {47|giving them names, and} passing them down through families.

{48|Some bakers prefer packaged yeast because it is faster.} Researchers have collected starters from bakers around the world to study {49|its} microbes, hoping to understand how communities of tiny organisms work together. {50|}

reading.title: The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter
reading.intro: This passage is adapted from an original short story. The narrator, Leila, returns to the coastal town where she grew up.
paras: The bus left me at the edge of town just after four, when the light over the harbor had already begun to soften. I had imagined this moment for eleven years, and in every version I had pictured myself walking quickly, with purpose, toward my father's house. Instead I stood by the bus shelter for a long time, holding my suitcase with both hands, as if it might decide for me.

The town had changed in small, insulting ways. The bakery where I had bought sesame rolls every morning was now a phone shop. The wooden pier had been replaced by a concrete one, wider and safer and entirely without character. Only the lighthouse looked the same, white and patient at the end of the breakwater, the way it had looked in the photograph I had kept on every desk I had ever owned.

My father had kept that light for thirty years. When I was small he used to let me climb the spiral stairs with him at dusk, counting the steps aloud—one hundred and twelve—while he checked the lamp. He rarely spoke during those climbs. I took his silence for disapproval then; it was years before I understood that he was simply listening to the building, the way a doctor listens to a heartbeat.

We had argued, the summer I left, about whether I should go away to study engineering. He thought the city would swallow me. I thought the town already had. Neither of us said the things we meant, and for eleven years our letters had been polite and short, full of weather.

When I finally knocked, he opened the door before my hand had dropped. He was smaller than I remembered, and his hair had gone completely white. For a moment neither of us spoke. Then he looked past me, toward the lighthouse, and said, "The lamp has been giving me trouble. They want to replace it with an automatic one."

It was not the welcome I had rehearsed. But I set down my suitcase, and I heard myself say, "Let me take a look." He nodded once, as if this were the most ordinary thing in the world, and reached for his coat.

reading.title: The Economics of Free Shipping
reading.intro: This passage is adapted from an original article about consumer behavior.
paras: When online retailers first began offering free shipping, many analysts predicted that the practice would not last. Shipping a package costs money, after all, and someone has to pay for it. Yet free shipping has become so common that many shoppers now abandon their online carts when a delivery fee appears at checkout.

Behavioral economists argue that the appeal of free shipping has less to do with money than with how people perceive costs. In a typical experiment of this kind, shoppers are offered two versions of the same order. In the first, the products cost slightly more but shipping is free. In the second, the products are cheaper but a small shipping fee is added, making the total price identical. Typically, a clear majority choose the first option, even though they would pay exactly the same amount.

Researchers explain this preference using the idea of the "zero price effect." When something costs nothing, people tend to treat it not just as cheap but as a different category altogether—a gift rather than a purchase. A fee, however small, feels like a loss, and people are generally more sensitive to losses than to equivalent gains.

Retailers have learned to use this tendency strategically. Many offer free shipping only on orders above a certain amount, such as 50 dollars. Shoppers whose carts fall just below the threshold often add another item rather than pay a few dollars for delivery. In effect, the "free" shipping encourages customers to spend more than they had planned.

Free shipping is not truly free, of course. Its cost is usually built into product prices or covered by higher spending. Some economists also point to costs that do not appear on any receipt: more delivery trucks on the road, more packaging waste, and more items returned and shipped again. A few retailers have begun experimenting with alternatives, such as rewarding customers who choose slower delivery or combine their orders into a single shipment.
Whether such efforts will change shoppers' habits is uncertain. What is clear is that a single word—"free"—can shape decisions far more powerfully than a careful comparison of prices would suggest.

reading.title: Two Views of the Public Library
reading.intro: Passage A is adapted from an original essay by a librarian. Passage B is adapted from an original essay by an architect.
paras: PASSAGE A

People sometimes ask whether libraries still matter now that so much information is online. The question assumes that a library is mainly a place to find information. It never was. A library is a place where anyone may sit for as long as they like without being asked to buy anything. In most cities, that makes it almost unique.

On a typical afternoon in my branch, a retired engineer reads newspapers in four languages, two students rehearse a debate in a study room, and a man who recently lost his job uses our computers to apply for work. None of them would describe what they are doing as "finding information." They are using a public space that asks nothing of them except respect for others.
That is why I worry when libraries are judged only by how many books they lend. A library that lends fewer books but welcomes more people is not failing. It is doing what it was always meant to do.
PASSAGE B

For most of their history, public libraries were designed around books. Reading rooms were quiet, shelves dominated the floor, and the building's grandest space was often the one that held the most volumes. The architecture announced that knowledge was precious and should be approached with care.

Many recent libraries reverse these priorities. Shelves move to the edges, and the center fills with flexible spaces: rooms that can host a coding class in the morning and a concert in the evening, kitchens for cooking demonstrations, studios for recording music. Some critics complain that such buildings feel more like community centers than libraries.

I think the critics misunderstand what a library's architecture should express. The older buildings honored books because books were the main way people shared knowledge. Today knowledge is shared in many forms, and a library that makes room for all of them is not abandoning its mission. It is carrying that mission into a new century.

reading.title: How Octopuses See Color Without Seeing Color
reading.intro: This passage is adapted from an original article about animal vision.
paras: Octopuses are masters of camouflage. Within a fraction of a second, an octopus can change the color and pattern of its skin to match rocks, sand, or coral. Yet for decades this ability posed a puzzle, because most octopus species appear to be color-blind. Their eyes contain only one type of light-sensitive cell, or photoreceptor, which means they should be unable to tell colors apart the way humans do.

Humans have three types of cone photoreceptors, each most sensitive to a different range of wavelengths. The brain compares signals from the three types to identify color. With only one type of photoreceptor, an animal can detect brightness but, according to the standard view, cannot distinguish one hue from another of equal brightness.

In 2016, a father-and-son team of researchers proposed a possible solution. They noted that octopus pupils come in unusual shapes—U-shaped, W-shaped, or dumbbell-shaped—rather than round. These shapes allow light to enter the eye from many angles. Because a lens bends different wavelengths of light by slightly different amounts, an effect called chromatic aberration, light of different colors comes into sharp focus at slightly different distances from the lens.

The researchers suggested that an octopus might exploit this effect. By adjusting the distance between its lens and its retina, an octopus could bring one color into focus at a time. An image that is sharp at one setting and blurry at another would reveal which wavelengths the object reflects. In this way, an animal with a single photoreceptor type could, in principle, extract color information.

The hypothesis has not yet been confirmed. Testing it requires measuring tiny changes in focus inside a living animal's eye, which is technically difficult. Some scientists also point out that octopus skin itself contains light-sensitive proteins similar to those in the eye, raising the possibility that the skin helps detect light directly.
Whatever the final explanation, the octopus is a reminder that animals may solve the same problem in very different ways. Color vision, it turns out, may not require the kind of eye that humans have.

science.title: Where Did the Moon Come From?
paras: Several observations constrain models of the Moon's origin: (1) The Moon's iron core is small, about 1–3% of its mass, compared with about 30% for Earth. (2) Moon rocks and Earth rocks have nearly identical ratios of oxygen isotopes. (3) The Earth–Moon system spins and orbits with an unusually large amount of angular momentum. Two scientists present different models.

Scientist 1: Early in Earth's history, a Mars-sized body collided with the young Earth at an angle. The impact blasted material from the outer, rocky layers of both bodies into orbit, where it gathered to form the Moon. Because the debris came mostly from rocky outer layers, the Moon received little iron. The collision also gave the system its large angular momentum. Mixing of material during the impact explains why the isotopes match.

Scientist 2: The Moon formed alongside Earth from the same disk of dust and gas that surrounded the young Sun. Because both bodies formed from the same local material, their oxygen isotopes match naturally, without requiring a collision. The Moon's small core results from the Moon forming in a region where most iron had already been gathered into the growing Earth. The large angular momentum was acquired gradually from material falling onto the system.

c: the Moon contains relatively little iron compared with Earth.

steps: Compare the claim or model with the data or viewpoint, one statement at a time.
Both accept the small core as an observation to explain.
Only Scientist 1 proposes an impact, and neither proposes capture or different isotopes.
Answer: the Moon contains relatively little iron compared with Earth.

steps: Compare the claim or model with the data or viewpoint, one statement at a time.

Answer: it formed mainly from material blasted from rocky outer layers.

math.stem:
2^(x + 3) = 4^(x + 2)
What value of x satisfies the equation above?
steps: Same base, so set the exponents equal: x + 3 = 2x + 4.
math.key: Rewrite both sides with the same base, then set the exponents equal.

math.stem:
k(x − 4) = 3x − 2
In the equation above, k is a constant. For what value of k does the equation have no solution?
steps: A linear equation has no solution when the x-coefficients on both sides match but the constants do not.
Check the constants with k = 3: left side −4(3) = −12, right side −2. They differ, so there is no solution.
math.key: No solution: same coefficient of x on both sides, different constants. Infinitely many: both the same.

math.stem: Which expression is equivalent to (x⁶ · x⁻⁴) / x⁸, for x ≠ 0?
steps: Multiplying powers with the same base: add exponents. x⁶ · x⁻⁴ = x².
Dividing: subtract exponents. x² / x⁸ = x⁻⁶.
A negative exponent means a reciprocal: x⁻⁶ = 1/x⁶.
math.key: Multiply → add exponents; divide → subtract exponents; negative exponent → reciprocal.

math.stem:
Data set A: 25, 40, 55, 70, 85
Data set B: 51, 53, 55, 57, 59
Which statement correctly compares the two data sets?
choices: They have the same mean, and data set B has a smaller standard deviation.
They have the same mean, and data set A has a smaller standard deviation.
Data set B has a greater mean than data set A.
They have the same standard deviation.
steps: Mean of each set: 275 ÷ 5 = 55. The means are equal.
Standard deviation measures how spread out the values are around the mean.
Data set B's values are much closer to 55 than data set A's.
So data set B has the smaller standard deviation.
math.key: Standard deviation is about spread around the mean; compare it without calculating.

math.stem:

math.stem:
2x + 4y = 1
px + 8y = 5
In the system above, p is a constant. For what value of p does the system have no solution?
steps: No solution means the lines are parallel: same slope, different intercept.
The y-coefficients are in the ratio 8 ÷ 4 = 2, so the x-coefficients must be too: p = 2 × 2 = 4.
The constants are not in that ratio (2 × 1 = 2 differs from the second constant), so the lines are distinct.
math.key: No solution: coefficients proportional, constants not.

math.stem:
y > 3x + 3
y ≤ 2x + 5
Which point (x, y) is a solution to the system of inequalities above?
steps: A solution must make both inequalities true.
Each other point fails at least one of the inequalities when its coordinates are substituted.
math.key: Test each point in every inequality; one failure rules it out.

math.stem:
2x + 6y = −3
px + 18y = −6
In the system above, p is a constant. For what value of p does the system have no solution?
steps: No solution means the lines are parallel: same slope, different intercept.
The y-coefficients are in the ratio 18 ÷ 6 = 3, so the x-coefficients must be too: p = 3 × 2 = 6.
The constants are not in that ratio (3 × (−3) = −9 differs from the second constant), so the lines are distinct.
math.key: No solution: coefficients proportional, constants not.

What is the minimum value of y for the equation above?
steps: The parabola opens upward (positive x² term), so its vertex gives the minimum.
math.key: For an upward parabola, the minimum is the y-value at x = −b/(2a).

math.stem: Which expression is equivalent to (x² − 25) / (x² − 2x − 35), for x ≠ 7 and x ≠ −5?
steps: Factor the numerator (difference of squares): x² − 25 = (x − 5)(x + 5).
Factor the denominator: find two numbers with product −35 and sum −2: 5 and −7, so x² − 2x − 35 = (x + 5)(x − 7).
Cancel the common factor (x + 5), allowed because x ≠ −5.
math.key: Factor completely, then cancel common factors, never common terms.

math.stem: Researchers randomly selected 600 employees at a large company and asked whether they use a flexible schedule. Those who said yes showed higher average job satisfaction. Which conclusion is best supported by the study?
choices: A flexible schedule is associated with higher average job satisfaction among employees at a large company, but a cause cannot be determined.
A flexible schedule is likely to cause higher average job satisfaction among employees at a large company.
A flexible schedule is likely to cause higher average job satisfaction for volunteers like these, but the result may not apply to all employees at a large company.
A flexible schedule is associated with higher average job satisfaction among these volunteers; the result may not apply to all employees at a large company, and a cause cannot be determined.
steps: Random sampling? Yes. Results can be generalized to employees at a large company.
Random assignment? No (people chose for themselves). Only an association can be claimed; other factors could explain it.
Combine both: A flexible schedule is associated with higher average job satisfaction among employees at a large company, but a cause cannot be determined.
math.key: Random sampling → generalize to the population. Random assignment → cause and effect.

math.stem: In trapezoid ABCD shown, AB ∥ CD and the diagonals meet at E. If AE = 3, AC = 11, and CD = 24, what is the length of AB?
steps: Because AB ∥ CD, triangles ABE and CDE are similar (alternate interior angles are equal).
Corresponding sides are proportional: AB/CD = AE/EC, so AB/24 = 3/8.
math.key: Parallel sides in a trapezoid create similar triangles at the intersection of the diagonals.

math.stem: Which set of side lengths, in inches, could be the sides of an obtuse triangle?
steps: Compare a² + b² with c², where c is the longest side.
a² + b² > c² → acute; a² + b² = c² → right; a² + b² < c² → obtuse (and a + b > c so a triangle exists).
For 5, 6, 9: 5² + 6² = 61 and 9² = 81, so the triangle is obtuse.
math.key: Classify triangles by comparing a² + b² with c².

math.stem: Which set of side lengths, in inches, could be the sides of an acute triangle?
steps: Compare a² + b² with c², where c is the longest side.
a² + b² > c² → acute; a² + b² = c² → right; a² + b² < c² → obtuse (and a + b > c so a triangle exists).
For 5, 6, 7: 5² + 6² = 61 and 7² = 49, so the triangle is acute.
math.key: Classify triangles by comparing a² + b² with c².

math.stem: Which set of side lengths, in inches, could be the sides of a right triangle?
steps: Compare a² + b² with c², where c is the longest side.
a² + b² > c² → acute; a² + b² = c² → right; a² + b² < c² → obtuse (and a + b > c so a triangle exists).
For 3, 4, 5: 3² + 4² = 25 and 5² = 25, so the triangle is right.
math.key: Classify triangles by comparing a² + b² with c².

math.stem: Two sides of a triangle have lengths 3 and 5. Which of the following could be the perimeter of the triangle?
steps: Triangle inequality: the third side c satisfies 2 < c < 8.
So the perimeter 3 + 5 + c is between 10 and 16, not including either end.
math.key: The third side is between the difference and the sum of the other two sides.

math.stem: A triangle has a perimeter of 30 cm. All three sides are whole numbers of centimeters, and the shortest side is 7 cm. How many different lengths are possible for the longest side?

math.stem: Which point lies on the set of all points equidistant from (2, -3) and (10, -3)?
steps: Points equidistant from two points lie on the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.
The segment is horizontal (both y = -3), with midpoint x = (2 + 10)/2 = 6.
The perpendicular bisector is the vertical line x = 6; only (6, 0) has x = 6.
math.key: Equidistant from two points ⇒ perpendicular bisector.

math.stem: What is the contrapositive of the statement “If an angle measures 30°, then it is acute”?
choices: If an angle is acute, then it measures 30°.
If an angle measures 30°, then it is not acute.
If an angle does not measure 30°, then it is not acute.
If an angle is not acute, then it does not measure 30°.
steps: Converse: If q, then p. Inverse: If not p, then not q. Contrapositive: If not q, then not p.
So the contrapositive is: If an angle is not acute, then it does not measure 30°.
Only the contrapositive always has the same truth value as the original statement.
math.key: Contrapositive ≡ original; converse ≡ inverse.

math.stem: A circular flower bed of radius 5√3 ft is inscribed in an equilateral triangle (each side is tangent to the circle). Bushes are planted at each vertex and every 6 ft along the sides. How many bushes are planted?
steps: For an equilateral triangle, inradius r = side/(2√3), so side = 2√3·r.
Bushes every 6 ft around a closed loop: 90 ÷ 6 = 15 (the vertices are included).
math.key: In an equilateral triangle the inradius is side/(2√3).

math.stem: If a, b, m, and n are integers with m < 0 and n > 0, and x² + mx + n = (x + a)(x + b), what must be true?
steps: Expand: (x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab.
So a + b = m and ab = n.
m < 0 gives a + b < 0; n > 0 gives ab > 0.

steps: Expand: (x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab.
So a + b = m and ab = n.
m < 0 gives a + b < 0; n < 0 gives ab < 0.
